- Model consistently overestimates prices, especially in early forecast periods (first 5–10 days of the 30-day window).
- Forecasts peak too early and then plateau or slightly decline, while true outcomes often show sharper, delayed peaks or more volatile corrections.
- After a spike in the history (e.g., 74+), model tends to overreact and overshoot, then gradually correct — but true outcomes often show a more abrupt or sustained correction.
- Model fails to capture mean reversion in the later half of the 30-day window — true outcomes frequently dip below 70 after a peak, while model stays near 71–73.
- Forecasts are too smooth; true outcomes show more jagged, asymmetric corrections — especially after 70–75 peaks.
- Model underestimates the magnitude of corrections after spikes — e.g., after 76.67, model drops only 1–2 points, while true drops 5–10 points.
- Model tends to ignore recent low values in history when forecasting — e.g., if history includes 60–65, model still forecasts 70+.
- Forecasts are too optimistic in the first 10 days, then become overly conservative — true outcomes often show a “rebound” or “reversal” after initial overestimation.
- Model doesn’t adjust for seasonality or policy-driven volatility — e.g., after 70–75 peaks, model doesn’t anticipate sharp drops due to regulatory or market intervention.
- Model’s forecast curve is too linear — true outcomes show non-linear, often exponential decay or sudden drops after peaks.
